newsitem.title: GERMANY: Tietmeyer-Durability overrides three pct EMU goal.
newsitem.headline: Tietmeyer-Durability overrides three pct EMU goal.

text.p: Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said on Sunday he hoped Germany could meet the Maastricht Treaty deficit goal this year but said sustainable budgetary discipline was more important than hitting targets.
"I very much hope that this country will be in a position to meet the criteria," Tietmeyer told German radio. A text of the interview was made available in advance.
"The three percent (deficit to GDP ratio set down in the Maastricht Treaty) is an important reference number -- there is no doubt of that," he continued.

"But more important than the one-off fulfilment, or bare undershooting or overshooting of this number, is the question as to whether countries' public finances ... are in a condition that can be viewed as sustainable, and lastingly sustainable."
Tietmeyer said a convincing reform of the German tax system was essential to get the economy in shape.
Tietmeyer said also that revaluing gold lodged at the Bundesbank would not under current rules yield any payout to the government.

Asked how Finance Minister Theo Waigel could benefit from Bundesbank gold reserves, Tietmeyer said: "According to the rules applying, this would only work if gold reserves were to be sold. But the government has made clear that it will not in any way force the Bundesbank to sell gold. To that extent it is not an issue at all."

The Bundesbank has reached an agreement with the government over revaluing currency reserves lodged at the central bank which will not generate any extraordinary payout to Bonn this year, the crucial year for the choice of participants in monetary union.
The central bank earlier shot down a plan by Waigel to use revaluation of reserves to ease Germany's path to monetary union.
Tietmeyer repeated that the compromise reached with Bonn, viewed widely as a come-down for the government, was a "good and acceptable solution."
